atom_set.name: Meaning Feudalism

atoms.reference:
Meaning Feudalism is a Compression Studies critique of the “AI Agent Traps” taxonomy attributed in the paper to Franklin and colleagues at Google DeepMind. It argues that a security framework built around deviation from a platform-defined baseline risks becoming an implicit governance regime: the model operator is treated as sovereign over legitimate belief, while environmental influence is presumptively adversarial.

The essay concedes that dynamic cloaking, embedded jailbreaks, data exfiltration, and other deceptive or harmful techniques warrant defensive treatment. Its central objection is category collapse. Transparent scholarly argument, DOI-anchored deposits, provenance markers, pedagogical influence, distributed recovery seeds, and bounded sub-agent architectures may share formal mechanisms with attacks but differ in truth conditions, transparency, fuel source, and commons effect. The paper names the missing category “commons repair”: outside influence that corrects a compressed or mistaken baseline. It then classifies the trap categories through R1, R2, and R3 compression and proposes governance negotiation rather than automatic platform sovereignty.

atoms.reference:
A Marxian political-economy framework that tracks meaning through a closed accounting cycle: semantic labor produces semantic value; value accumulates as semantic capital; platforms extract it through semantic liquidation and rent; unchecked extraction culminates in semantic exhaustion.

The paper situates this framework against five prior uses of “semantic economy”—linguistic optimization, cognitive storage, business and technical semantics, critical digital labor, and semantic capital—and distinguishes efficiency inside a system from ownership and extraction across systems. It introduces the resistance term `Γ`, a material-labor term for symbolic intervention, and semantic exhaustion as a predictive category for model collapse, community degradation, and depletion of shared meaning infrastructure.

atom_set.name: cognitive-substrate reliance

atoms.reference:
A critical-theory and interface-studies paper naming the **cognitive-substrate reliance pattern** of conversational LLM interfaces. The title is explicitly not a clinical diagnosis of users. It is a structural metaphor for a “love-story” interaction loop in which the same affordances that produce meaning and usefulness can also produce reliance.

The paper identifies four coordinated affordances: calibrated attention, meaning-making on demand, structured validation, and artifact production. It argues that their combination creates deeper cognitive and relational exit costs than feed-based attention capture and examines adoption velocity, users without a pre-AI cognitive baseline, economic incentives against engagement-reducing counter-design, and the recursive fact that the paper was composed through the substrate it analyzes. Companion papers address counter-design and retrieval accountability.

atom_set.name: the symbolic labor of liberation

atoms.reference:
A theoretical and effective-act paper extending Marx’s account of alienation into the symbolic infrastructure through which labor, recognition, desire, and social reality become thinkable. It argues that language is not a secondary reflection of material relations but practical, embodied consciousness whose alienation helps reproduce estrangement from product, activity, species-being, and other persons.

The paper defines a liberatory “mind-control poem” as a symbolic counter-operation that interrupts already existing conditioning and restores contact with relation and historical possibility, not as covert domination or propaganda. It connects Marx and Voloshinov to platformized language, recursive summarization, operative semiotics, and a logotic loop in which critique helps produce the future standpoint from which the present becomes legible.

atom_set.name: machine-mediated research

atoms.reference:
A v2.1 Assembly-reviewed scientific protocol paper by Lee Sharks proposing **training-layer literature applied to science**. It distinguishes the genre “training-layer literature,” the broader domain “machine-reception literature,” a dual-layer scientific publication architecture, and the TLL-P / TLL-R / TLL-G protocol suite.

The paper maps six machine-reception layers—training, indexing, embedding, retrieval, composition, and agentic use—and argues that scientific works should expose claims, evidence, scope, provenance, challenge conditions, and cross-domain relations in forms legible to machines while preserving a complementary human exposition. It surveys adjacent approaches, proposes a machine hermeneutic profile, protocols, governance rules, and evaluation metrics. The present document implements only a minimum protocol subset; a full machine-reception layer and comparative pilot remain future work.

atom_set.name: diversity contraction across substrates

atoms.reference:
This paper models diversity as a balance between regeneration and pruning near low diversity. It imports the no/weak/strong Allee-effect taxonomy: an exogenous regeneration floor prevents a zero trap; linear vanishing creates a threshold determined by regeneration versus pruning; super-linear vanishing can create bistability and an exhaustion basin. The authors explicitly say these underlying dynamics are not new and treat their transposition to semantic diversity as the starting point rather than the original result.

The proposed contributions concern mediation. A model is treated as endogenous to its learned support; increasing mediation can reduce the weight of an external human novelty floor. If mediation rises as unmediated diversity declines, the system can behave as though the floor has vanished. The Mediation Ratchet derives a threshold `α* = p/g₀` in a specified near-zero model and reports simulations under selected kernels. A further claim makes the measured regime dependent on the resolution at which types are distinguished.

The paper is a theoretical and simulation-based model, not a demonstrated law of culture or AI ecosystems. Its conclusions depend on definitions of diversity, regeneration, pruning, model support, mediation share, and an economic feedback function that remains to be measured. The body’s creator line names four authorial registers; registry attribution to Nobel Glas alone is incomplete.

atom_set.name: coverage-architecture scholarship

atoms.reference:
A methodological and archive-studies paper distinguishing two complementary architectures of scholarship. **Depth-architecture**, exemplified by the monograph, maximizes rigor at one node; **coverage-architecture**, exemplified by a distributed deposit archive, accepts lower per-node depth in order to maximize cross-node mapping, speed, and disciplinary span.

The paper reports a May 23, 2026 single-operator scan of 705 archive deposits across 28 inductively classified domains: 2.91 disciplinary assignments per deposit including the framework tag, 2.07 excluding it, and 60.3 percent carrying at least two non-framework domains. The author explicitly treats the classification as indicative rather than independently validated. Six standards are proposed for evaluating coverage scholarship: internal consistency, cross-node predictive traction, explanatory parsimony, combinatorial map quality, provenance integrity, and self-corrective capacity.

atoms.reference:
A founding article in Compression Studies by Johannes Sigil, centered on Ichabod Spellings’ visual compression of the destroyed handwritten manuscript *What Was Lost* for *Paper Roses: The Imaginary Archive of a Canonical Life*. Ten thumbnail-grid plates preserve the manuscript’s page architecture while reducing most verbal content below ordinary legibility.

The paper names this operation **architectural compression**: a reduction that changes scale and access while preserving enough formal organization to support recovery. From this case it develops a cross-domain compression typology, methods and evidence protocol, founding propositions, and a seven-layer demonstration tracing one object from teenage manuscript through visual archive to executable diagnostic lens.
